title: The Trump Administration Is Attacking Federal Workers with Disabilities
author: Hayley Brown
content:
As Disability Pride Month comes to a close, the Trump administration has
marked the occasion by making it difficult-to-impossible for disabled federal
workers to do their work. Workers from
[multiple](https://www.govexec.com/workforce/2026/06/nsf-using-its-hq-move-
revoke-telework-workers-disabilities-employees-say/414278/)
[agencies](https://www.govexec.com/workforce/2025/09/cdc-ends-telework-
employees-disabilities-union-says/408188/) allege that the Trump
administration has been systematically [denying or
stalling](https://federalnewsnetwork.com/workforce/2026/06/nteu-sues-treasury-
hhs-over-thousands-of-stalled-telework-requests-from-disabled-employees/)
accommodation requests and
[rescinding](https://www.govexec.com/workforce/2026/07/disabled-veterans-
losing-telework-accommodations-harder-working-va/414626/) telework as an
accommodation. Several employees say they have [faced
retaliation](https://www.govexec.com/workforce/2026/06/lawsuit-claims-doj-
retaliating-against-employees-disabilities-who-request-telework/413955/) for
requesting telework accommodations in the first place.

When the second Trump administration took office, one of its first moves was
to [mandate a return to in-person
work](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/return-to-in-
person-work/) for federal workers. While the order noted that the memorandum
should be “implemented consistent with applicable law,” that part has been
interpreted generously. Having moved to [discard collective bargaining
agreements](https://cepr.net/publications/disability-is-not-disposable-
neither-is-labor/) that established remote work benefits, the Trump
administration is now eliminating telework accommodations for disabled federal
workers who rely on them. While there may be good reasons to prefer in-person
work in specific instances, the administration’s blanket approach appears
designed to demoralize workers, with discriminatory consequences for disabled
workers.

Many workers in the US are protected by the Americans with Disabilities Act
(ADA), which prohibits discrimination and requires covered employers to
reasonably accommodate employees with disabilities on the job. The ADA also
establishes accessibility and nondiscrimination requirements for state and
local government services and many businesses open to the public. Title 1 of
the ADA, however, expressly excludes “the United States” and wholly owned
federal corporations from its definition of an employer. Those who work for
federal agencies and the US Postal Service are nevertheless afforded similar
protections under Section 501 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, which
actually goes beyond the ADA in requiring the US government to take
affirmative action to recruit and retain disabled workers. It is likely
because of this that [disabled workers are overrepresented in the federal
government](https://cepr.net/publications/disability-is-not-disposable-
neither-is-labor/).

Trump administration officials justified the return-to-office requirements by
claiming that telework was being “abused,”
[conflating](https://www.afge.org/publication/setting-the-record-straight-
about-telework-use-by-federal-employees/) being in the office with “going to
work” in a way that implied that remotely performed work somehow didn’t count.
They also claimed, without evidence, that telework was [negatively affecting
productivity](https://www.opm.gov/news/secrets-of-opm/why-showing-up-counts/).
In fact, telework has been associated with [increased
productivity](https://www.bls.gov/opub/btn/volume-13/remote-work-
productivity.htm) and [improved
morale](https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2024/06/hybrid-work-is-a-win-win-
win-for-companies-workers) in a [variety of
contexts](https://www.worktime.com/blog/statistics/remote-work-productivity-
statistics-trends-data), including
[some](https://cep.lse.ac.uk/_NEW/publications/abstract.asp?index=11155) in
the [public sector](https://allwork.space/2024/05/new-report-shows-telework-
boosted-federal-employee-morale-after-years-of-decline-as-policies-are-under-
review-in-washington/). Flexible telework policies are also an excellent
example of [universal design](https://cepr.net/publications/how-unions-can-
use-universal-design-to-better-serve-workers-with-disabilities/), an approach
that, when possible, reframes accommodations as benefits for all staff. This
helps reduce stigma and resentment while improving working conditions for
workers with and without disabilities. In the case of telework, those without
disabilities who simply perform better working remotely have the opportunity
to do what helps them thrive. A [recent survey of federal
workers](https://federalnewsnetwork.com/workforce/2026/07/after-returning-to-
the-office-federal-employees-report-low-productivity-morale/) bears this out,
as morale and productivity have plummeted since the enforcement of return-to-
office measures.

It is also reasonable to think that achieving those survey results was the
intended purpose all along. The back-to-the-office edict appeared alongside a
host of other measures to demoralize and ultimately drive workers out of the
federal government. Office of Management and Budget Director [Russ Vought
didn’t mince words](https://www.propublica.org/article/video-donald-trump-
russ-vought-center-renewing-america-maga) with respect to federal employees:
“When they wake up in the morning, we want them to not want to go to work.… We
want to put them in trauma.” Vought’s hope was, in part, to destroy the
federal bureaucracy’s capacity to enforce federal regulations (“…so that the
EPA can’t do all of the rules against our energy industry”) that protect the
public good.

The trauma the administration has inflicted has hit disabled federal workers
especially hard. The poor treatment of disabled federal workers is also taking
place amid the Trump administration’s attacks on people with disabilities more
broadly. These include [a recent memorandum from the Department of Justice
(DOJ)](https://www.justice.gov/olc/media/1446701/dl) that argued, despite
[decades of legal
precedent](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/527/581/), that states
are not obligated to provide home- and community-based care to disabled people
who require such support to remain in their communities. Advocates warn such
an approach could result in a [return to mass exclusion and
institutionalization](https://www.npr.org/2026/06/20/nx-s1-5865100/doj-memo-
trump-disability-civil-rights-institutionalization), resulting in the de facto
segregation of people with disabilities from society.

If there is one bright spot, it is that the unions that represent federal
workers with disabilities are fighting to [defend their
rights](https://federalnewsnetwork.com/workforce/2026/06/nteu-sues-treasury-
hhs-over-thousands-of-stalled-telework-requests-from-disabled-employees/).
Unions can play a [critical role](https://cepr.net/publications/why-union-
membership-is-good-for-workers-with-disabilities/) in upholding the rights of
disabled people by making it easier for workers to hold employers accountable.
Unions are also associated with [wage and benefit premiums for disabled
workers](https://cepr.net/publications/the-union-advantage-for-workers-with-
disabilities-higher-pay-more-benefits/). This is one reason why [increasing
unionization](https://cepr.net/publications/increase-unionization/) is part of
[CEPR’s Majority Agenda](https://cepr.net/publications/the-majority-agenda-
good-jobs-strong-infrastructure-fair-play/), which highlights broadly popular
policy changes that would meaningfully improve the lives of working people.

Ultimately, the federal workforce benefits from the contributions of disabled
workers, and pushing them out by denying accommodations is both cruel and a
loss for the public they serve. The Trump administration is shortchanging
everyone by stripping disabled public servants of the accommodations they need
to keep serving.

_This first appeared on[CEPR](http://www.cepr.net)._
